tagline.text: Iloilo's signature seafood restaurant on Villa Beach

location.label: Location
location.text: Molo-Arevalo Boulevard, Villa de Arevalo district (Villa Beach), Iloilo City

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱400–1,500 (per person for a meal; based on a single Sept 2025 review, 10% service charge extra, confirm locally)

children.text: A signature Iloilo seafood restaurant open since 1986, where you can enjoy fresh seafood from live tanks on Villa Beach with a view of the Iloilo Strait. Grilled managat, aligue rice and baked oysters are the best-known dishes.

Breakthrough Restaurant is a seafood restaurant on Villa Beach (Villa Baybay) in the Villa de Arevalo district on the south side of Iloilo City. It is an open-air restaurant facing the Iloilo Strait, with Guimaras Island visible across the water, and it is said to be a place every local and visitor stops at once. Wikipedia describes Villa Beach as a long urban gray-sand beach and mentions the restaurant among the beach's best-known seafood places. Travelers coming from Manila often choose it for their first evening in Iloilo or their last meal before leaving.

According to a 2009 Philippine Daily Inquirer article, marine biologist Raymundo Robles started it with about ₱20,000 in capital. It began as a small snack bar on E. Lopez Street in the Jaro district, and the story goes that as customers asked for fresh seafood, the tanks multiplied until the restaurant looked like an aquarium. His wife, Isabel Saldajeno-Robles, studied hotel and restaurant management. It moved to its current Villa Beach location in 1992, and the regional tourism office is said to have named it Best Restaurant in Western Visayas in 2006 and 2007.

The biggest draw is the live tanks. According to the Inquirer article, around 30 cement-and-glass aquariums and indoor ponds hold abalone, catfish, crabs, lobsters, shrimps, shellfish and angel wing clams, with salinity and water quality adjusted to resemble natural habitats. You can pick what you want and ask for it grilled, steamed or in a soup, or order turo-turo style by pointing at the dishes you want. Signature dishes are charcoal-grilled managat (red snapper) served with sinamak vinegar sauce, aligue rice and baked oysters.

The building is made of bamboo, cogon grass, nipa palm and rattan reinforced with cement, and it stretches along the shoreline, reportedly seating about 1,000 diners at a time. The seafood is said to come from suppliers in Capiz, Antique, Negros Occidental and General Santos. The travel blog Our Awesome Planet compared this restaurant with Tatoy's, another popular Iloilo restaurant, and concluded that rather than picking a winner you should try both. It is a single restaurant, but it covers the beach, the sunset and a seafood meal in one stop, which makes it worth a place in your Iloilo itinerary.

Live crabs, shrimps, shellfish and more are on display, and you choose them and have them grilled, steamed or made into soup. For items priced by weight, be sure to ask for the price before you order.

The restaurant says it helped make local managat famous, and it is the signature dish. You dip it in sinamak, a vinegar-based sauce. Availability and price may vary day to day, so check before you order.
This rich rice with the flavor of crab fat is a regular on reviewers' lists and is often ordered with grilled seafood. It is good for sharing among your group.
Oysters come steamed or oven-baked with garlic and cheese. Ilonggos also dip oysters in sinamak mixed with soy sauce and calamansi.

The restaurant's own listing features pancit Molo (Molo-style dumpling noodle soup), imbao clam soup and baked scallops. The Inquirer article also lists binakol chicken soup and banana blossom salad as signature dishes.
From the open-air seats you can see the Iloilo Strait and the view toward Guimaras Island. Go around sunset to enjoy a table on the sea side.
After the meal, you can stroll along the nearby Villa Beach. The beach is described as the venue of the Paraw Regatta Festival in February.

According to the Inquirer article, the regional tourism office named it Best Restaurant in Western Visayas in 2006 and 2007. This backs its long-standing reputation, but for current quality check recent reviews.

items.title: Sunset dinner
items.subtitle: Arrive before sunset and eat at a relaxed pace

children.text: Head from central Iloilo to Villa de Arevalo by Grab or taxi. The trip from the city center is usually quoted at about
20–30 minutes
Arrive and ask for a table with a sea view. Tables fill up quickly before sunset, so it is better to come early.
Look around the live tanks at the entrance and decide on the seafood of the day and how it is cooked. For items priced by weight, ask the price first.

Before ordering, compare the day's seafood and prices at the tanks and decide whether to have it grilled, steamed or in soup. Dishes can take a while to arrive after you order, so start with something light such as oysters or a salad.
Order grilled managat, baked oysters, aligue rice, pancit Molo and more, and share them.
After the meal, take a short walk on Villa Beach and return to your lodging by Grab.
Opening hours are quoted as either 9 AM or 10 AM to 9 PM depending on the source, so confirm before you visit.

items.title: Lunch route
items.subtitle: Go during the day and eat cool

children.text: If you arrive before the lunch rush, the wait is short. Some reviews say it gets hot during the day because there is no air conditioning, so bring a hat and water.
Order a soup dish and grilled items together. With a larger group, it is better to share several plates.
After the meal, stroll along Villa Beach or head back to your sightseeing in central Iloilo.
There are direct flights from Manila (MNL) to Iloilo International Airport (ILO), and the flight is known to take about
1 hour 20–30 minutes
. Check airline timetables when you book.
The airport is about
20km
from central Iloilo.

From the city to Villa, we recommend Grab or a taxi. Check jeepney routes locally.
It takes about
20–30 minutes
from central Iloilo by Grab or metered taxi.
The address is Molo-Arevalo Boulevard, Barangay Santo Niño (Villa Beach), and the phone number is (033) 337 3027.
Grab and metered taxis operate, and fares vary with distance and time of day, so check locally.

As a restaurant it can be visited in any season, but it is open-air, so it is hot during the day and can be affected by wind and rain in the rainy season. Evenings in the November–May dry season are the most comfortable.

In February the Paraw Regatta Festival takes place on Villa Beach, so the beach and the restaurant can be crowded. Shellfish such as oysters and diwal may not be on the menu depending on the season and harvest rules, so it is wise to call ahead.

Lunch and dinner are said to be the busiest times. To get a table before sunset, arrive around 5 PM; for a quieter meal, come just before lunch or early in the evening. Opening hours are quoted as 9 AM or 10 AM to 9 PM depending on the source, so confirm locally.

blocks.label: Season at a glance
rows: The evening sea breeze is pleasant. It is crowded during the Paraw Regatta in February.
Very hot during the day, so we recommend visiting around sunset.
Open-air seating can get wet, so check the weather before you go.

Villa Beach has resorts and beachside restaurants, and another well-known seafood restaurant, Tatoy's, is nearby. Staying on the beach side makes it easy to walk back after dinner, but you will need another ride for sightseeing in the city. See the lodging information in the Iloilo City entry as well.

At this restaurant you get the widest variety by sharing grilled dishes, oysters, scallops and roast chicken or pork among several people. A September 2025 review listed baked oysters at ₱220, sizzling crab meat at ₱300, lechon pork at ₱300, caldereta at ₱380 and lechon chicken at ₱390. A 2017 article listed oysters at ₱60 steamed and ₱120 baked, so prices have risen a lot in a few years. One review said the restaurant took cash only, so bring plenty of cash.
If you have more time, you can try noodle dishes such as pancit Molo or caldo elsewhere in the city on the same day and compare them with what you eat here.
Arrive early if you want a sea-side seat at sunset.
Bring plenty of cash. Reviews differ on whether cards are accepted, so check.
Live-tank seafood is priced by weight, so confirm the price and cooking method before you order.
It is best to order several plates and share them. Many reviews say portions are generous.
Try dipping the oysters in sinamak mixed with soy sauce and calamansi.
Shellfish such as diwal may not be available depending on the harvest period, so check by phone.
The open-air dining area has no air conditioning and can be hot during the day. Bring a hat and light clothing.
Grab is the easiest way back. Calls can be heavy in the evening, so book one as you finish your meal.
If shuttling back and forth from a city lodging is a hassle, plan around a beach-side lodging or a morning visit.
If you are a large group, call ahead with your numbers and time to make seating easier. Check locally whether reservations are possible.
Live-tank items are priced at market rates, and some are very expensive. One reviewer recorded lobster at ₱6,000 per kilo. Be sure to confirm the total price before you order.
Opening hours and menu prices change. Check the latest information by phone or on the official page before you visit.
Prices in this entry are approximate figures based on 2025–2026 reviews.
When you go as a large group or on weekend or holiday evenings, the wait can be long.
Be mindful of freshness and your own constitution with shellfish and raw items, and if it is your first time, start with grilled or steamed dishes.
Villa Beach is an urban beach, so check locally whether swimming is possible and how the water quality is, and treat it mainly as a place for a walk.
If you have a seafood allergy, tell staff about the cooking method and sauces in advance. Sauces used on grilled dishes and the condiments served alongside may contain seafood ingredients.
The central city of Western Visayas, usually about
20–30 minutes
from the restaurant, with churches, heritage houses and many places to eat.
The mango island visible across the water from the restaurant, which you can reach by boat.
The urban gray-sand beach in front of the restaurant, which hosts the Paraw Regatta Festival in February.
A riverside promenade near the city center, good for a light walk after a meal.
